ibu — exploring 6.79 million screening mammograms¶

FRE 6191 · Data Visualization · Final project notebook Azfina Putri Anindita

ibu means "mother" in Indonesian. My mom had breast cancer and is healthy today, so I wanted to understand the women who sit in the mammogram chair. This notebook is my exploration: I look at the data, try ideas, keep what shows a real pattern and drop what does not. The best charts became the Dash app (app.py).

Story question: Who is in the mammogram chair — and how is she changing?

Business angle: a screening provider (clinic network, imaging center, or a women's-health brand) needs to know who its patients are, how that mix is moving, and which groups need a different message.

1. Research questions and hypotheses¶

# Research question My hypothesis before looking
RQ1 How has the screened population changed from 2005 to 2017? H1: women being screened are getting older, heavier and more diverse, and fewer use hormone therapy (HRT).
RQ2 Who has dense breasts (the tissue that can hide tumours)? H2: density falls with age and with BMI, and it differs by race even at the same age.
RQ3 Are breast-cancer survivors a growing part of screening — and is that only because women are older? H3: the survivor share rises, and it still rises after removing the age effect.
RQ4 Which risk markers travel with a past breast cancer? H4: a family history goes with more prior cancer at every age.
RQ5 Does where you live matter — lifestyle (food, exercise, smoking) or money and insurance? H5a: states with unhealthier lifestyles (more obesity, smoking, inactivity, less fruit) have more breast cancer and more deaths. H5b: richer, better-insured states find more breast cancer but lose fewer women per case.

Section 9 checks each hypothesis against the data.

How this notebook flows¶

  1. Know the data (sections 3–4): what one row means, how the files fit, what is missing.
  2. Who is in the chair (section 5): first raw volume → then shares → age, race, HRT, obesity.
  3. What the scan sees (section 6): density — a first naive chart misleads me, so I switch to same-age comparisons.
  4. Who has been through it (section 7): survivors and risk markers, one dead end, then business segments.
  5. Where she lives (section 8): a second dataset, maps, regions, correlations and a small model.
  6. What I learned and how it became the dashboard (sections 9–10).

At several points I show a first try chart and then the better chart, because the first try taught me something.

2. Setup¶

I use pandas for the data and matplotlib for quick exploratory charts. Colours follow the ibu theme (plum and rose). Blue is used only as a "comparison" colour next to rose.

In [1]:
import glob, os
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib as mpl
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
%matplotlib inline

PLUM, ROSE, BLUE, INK, MUTED, GRID, LIGHT = "#4A1D3F", "#C2456E", "#5B6FB0", "#2E1027", "#6E4A64", "#E6DCE2", "#BFB3BA"
DENS_RAMP = ["#E58EA9", "#D0527A", "#A83A63", "#4A1D3F"]
mpl.rcParams.update({
    "figure.dpi": 110, "figure.figsize": (9, 4.2), "font.size": 10.5, "axes.titlesize": 12.5,
    "axes.titleweight": "bold", "axes.titlelocation": "left", "axes.titlecolor": INK,
    "axes.spines.top": False, "axes.spines.right": False, "axes.edgecolor": LIGHT,
    "axes.labelcolor": MUTED, "xtick.color": MUTED, "ytick.color": MUTED,
    "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.8, "axes.axisbelow": True,
    "legend.frameon": False,
})
DATA = "data"
pd.set_option("display.width", 140)


def dumbbell(ax, labels, a, b, an, bn, ca=BLUE, cb=ROSE, unit=" pts"):
    # one row per label: grey connector, two dots, the change written at the right
    y = np.arange(len(labels))
    ax.hlines(y, np.minimum(a, b), np.maximum(a, b), color=LIGHT, lw=3, zorder=1)
    ax.scatter(a, y, s=70, color=ca, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5, zorder=3, label=an)
    ax.scatter(b, y, s=70, color=cb, edgecolor="white", lw=1.5, zorder=3, label=bn)
    for yi, x0, x1 in zip(y, a, b):
        ax.text(max(x0, x1) + 0.8, yi, f"{x1 - x0:+.1f}{unit}", va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
    ax.set_yticks(y, labels); ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
    ax.set_xlim(0, max(max(a), max(b)) * 1.18)


def spread(ys, gap):
    # nudge end-of-line label positions apart so they never overlap (keeps their order)
    order = np.argsort(ys)
    out = np.array(ys, dtype=float)
    for k in range(1, len(order)):
        i, j = order[k], order[k - 1]
        out[i] = max(out[i], out[j] + gap)
    return out

3. Load the three files — are they three datasets or one?¶

The download came as three CSV files. Before anything else I need to know whether they are different samples or one dataset cut into pieces.

In [2]:
files = sorted(glob.glob(f"{DATA}/bcsc_risk_factors_summarized*.csv"))
raw = {os.path.basename(f): pd.read_csv(f) for f in files}
for name, d in raw.items():
    print(f"{name}: {d.shape[0]:>7,} rows · years {d.year.min()}–{d.year.max()} · {d['count'].sum():>9,} exams")

bcsc_risk_factors_summarized1_092020.csv: 509,410 rows · years 2013–2017 · 2,033,697 exams
bcsc_risk_factors_summarized2_092020.csv: 506,465 rows · years 2005–2009 · 2,539,649 exams
bcsc_risk_factors_summarized3_092020.csv: 506,465 rows · years 2009–2013 · 2,215,090 exams

Same 13 columns in every file and the years follow each other (2005–09, 2009–13, 2013–17). Thought: 2009 and 2013 appear in two files. If those rows were copies, joining the files would double-count them. Let me check.

In [3]:
keys = [c for c in next(iter(raw.values())).columns if c != "count"]
for yr in (2009, 2013):
    parts = [d[d.year == yr] for d in raw.values() if yr in d.year.values]
    shared = parts[0].merge(parts[1], on=keys)
    print(f"{yr}: rows in file A = {len(parts[0]):,}, file B = {len(parts[1]):,}, identical rows = {len(shared)}")

df = pd.concat(raw.values(), ignore_index=True)
print(f"\nCombined: {len(df):,} rows, {df['count'].sum():,} exams")

2009: rows in file A = 35,907, file B = 85,026, identical rows = 0
2013: rows in file A = 70,873, file B = 56,198, identical rows = 0

Combined: 1,522,340 rows, 6,788,436 exams

Finding: no row is in two files, and the combined total is exactly 6,788,436 exams — the number BCSC publishes for this dataset. So the three files are one dataset split by size, and stacking them is correct.

Important about the shape: each row is a combination of risk factors, and count says how many exams had that combination. Every percentage in this notebook is therefore weighted by count, never a plain row count.

Codebook (what the numbers mean)¶

Column Meaning Codes
year Calendar year of the exam 2005–2017
age_group_5_years Age group 1 = 18–29, 2 = 30–34 … 13 = 85+ (5-year steps)
race_eth Race / ethnicity 1 White, 2 Black, 3 Asian / Pacific Islander, 4 Native American, 5 Hispanic, 6 Other / mixed, 9 unknown
first_degree_hx Mother, sister or daughter had breast cancer 0 no, 1 yes, 9 unknown
age_menarche, age_first_birth Age at first period / first birth groups, 9 unknown
BIRADS_breast_density Breast density 1 A almost all fat, 2 B scattered, 3 C heterogeneously dense, 4 D extremely dense, 9 unknown
current_hrt Currently on hormone therapy 0 no, 1 yes, 9 unknown
menopaus Menopause status 1 pre/peri, 2 post, 3 surgical, 9 unknown
bmi_group Body-mass index 1 < 25, 2 25–29.9, 3 30–34.9, 4 35+, 9 unknown
biophx Ever had a breast biopsy 0 no, 1 yes, 9 unknown
breast_cancer_history Ever had breast cancer 0 no, 1 yes, 9 unknown
count Number of exams with exactly this combination 1 … thousands

Source: Breast Cancer Surveillance Consortium (BCSC) Risk Factors Dataset, summarized version (09/2020).

4. Data quality — how much is unknown?¶

Every risk-factor column uses the code 9 = unknown. I want to see how big that problem is per column.

In [5]:
LAB = {"race_eth": "Race / ethnicity", "first_degree_hx": "Family history", "age_menarche": "Age at first period",
       "age_first_birth": "Age at first birth", "BIRADS_breast_density": "Breast density", "current_hrt": "Hormone therapy",
       "menopaus": "Menopause status", "bmi_group": "BMI", "biophx": "Prior biopsy", "breast_cancer_history": "Prior breast cancer"}
w = df["count"]
unknown = pd.Series({lab: 100 * w[df[c] == 9].sum() / w.sum() for c, lab in LAB.items()}).sort_values()

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4.4))
DROP = ["Age at first period", "Age at first birth"]
cols = [ROSE if k in DROP else ("#E58EA9" if v > 30 else LIGHT) for k, v in unknown.items()]
ax.barh(unknown.index, unknown.values, color=cols, height=0.62)
for i, v in enumerate(unknown.values):
    ax.text(v + 0.8, i, f"{v:.0f}%", va="center", color=INK, fontsize=10)
ax.axvline(30, color=MUTED, lw=1, ls="--")
ax.set_xlabel("% of exams where the value is unknown")
ax.set_title("Three columns are over 30% unknown; I drop the two life-history ones (dark rose)")
ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Decision:

  • Drop age at first period and age at first birth. With a third to two-thirds unknown, any pattern could just be a pattern in who answered.
  • Keep the rest, and for each measure leave out only the exams where that measure is unknown (so BMI charts use exams with known BMI, and so on).
  • BMI is 36% unknown. I keep it but always say "where BMI is known".
  • Native American women are 0.3% of exams — too few to show alone — so I fold them into "Other / mixed".
In [6]:
df = df.drop(columns=["age_menarche", "age_first_birth"])
df = df.rename(columns={"age_group_5_years": "age", "race_eth": "race", "first_degree_hx": "fh",
                        "BIRADS_breast_density": "dens", "current_hrt": "hrt", "menopaus": "meno",
                        "bmi_group": "bmi", "biophx": "bx", "breast_cancer_history": "bch"})
df["race"] = df["race"].replace({4: 6})
df = df.groupby([c for c in df.columns if c != "count"], as_index=False)["count"].sum()   # smaller table

AGE_LAB = {1: "18–29", 2: "30–34", 3: "35–39", 4: "40–44", 5: "45–49", 6: "50–54", 7: "55–59", 8: "60–64",
           9: "65–69", 10: "70–74", 11: "75–79", 12: "80–84", 13: "85+"}
BAND = {1: "<40", 2: "<40", 3: "<40", 4: "40–49", 5: "40–49", 6: "50–59", 7: "50–59", 8: "60–69", 9: "60–69",
        10: "70+", 11: "70+", 12: "70+", 13: "70+"}
BANDS = ["<40", "40–49", "50–59", "60–69", "70+"]
RACE = {1: "White", 2: "Black", 3: "Asian / PI", 5: "Hispanic", 6: "Other / mixed"}
df["band"] = pd.Categorical(df.age.map(BAND), BANDS, ordered=True)


def share(d, flag, known, by=None):
    # count-weighted % of exams with `flag`, among exams where the measure is `known`
    d = d.assign(_n=d["count"] * flag(d), _d=d["count"] * known(d))
    if by is None:
        return 100 * d._n.sum() / d._d.sum()
    g = d.groupby(by, observed=True)[["_n", "_d"]].sum()
    return 100 * g._n / g._d

print(f"{len(df):,} rows after dropping the two columns and re-grouping")

403,814 rows after dropping the two columns and re-grouping

5. RQ1 — How is the screened population changing?¶

5a. First, the raw volume¶

In [7]:
per_year = df.groupby("year")["count"].sum() / 1e3
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.8))
ax.bar(per_year.index, per_year.values, color=ROSE, width=0.7)
ax.set_ylabel("Exams (thousands)")
ax.set_xticks(per_year.index)
ax.set_title(f"Exams per year peak in {per_year.idxmax()} and then fall by "
             f"{100 * (1 - per_year.iloc[-1] / per_year.max()):.0f}%")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Thought: this drop is not women skipping mammograms. BCSC says fewer facilities reported data in later years. So counts over time are misleading. From here on I compare shares (% of that year's exams), never totals. That rule carries into the dashboard.

5b. Age mix: first year vs last year¶

In [8]:
age = df.groupby(["year", "age"])["count"].sum().unstack(0)
age = 100 * age / age.sum()
x = np.arange(len(age))
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.2))
ax.bar(x - 0.2, age[2005], 0.4, color=BLUE, label="2005")
ax.bar(x + 0.2, age[2017], 0.4, color=ROSE, label="2017")
ax.set_xticks(x, [AGE_LAB[a] for a in age.index], rotation=0)
ax.set_ylabel("% of that year's exams")
ax.legend(loc="upper right")
older = age.loc[9:].sum()
ax.set_title(f"The chair is getting older: women 65+ were {older[2005]:.0f}% of exams in 2005, {older[2017]:.0f}% in 2017")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Thought: screening sits in the 40–74 core ages (as guidelines say), but the whole curve moves right. Because older women differ in many ways (less dense tissue, more past cancers), I must adjust for age later before comparing groups.

5c. Six traits over 13 years — first try¶

My first idea: put every trait on one chart.

In [9]:
TR = {
    "Hormone therapy (post-menopausal)": (lambda d: d.hrt == 1, lambda d: (d.hrt != 9) & (d.meno == 2)),
    "Obese (BMI ≥ 30)": (lambda d: d.bmi.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.bmi != 9),
    "Dense breasts (C/D)": (lambda d: d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9),
    "Non-White (race known)": (lambda d: d.race.isin([2, 3, 5, 6]), lambda d: d.race != 9),
    "Prior breast cancer": (lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9),
    "Aged 65+": (lambda d: d.age >= 9, lambda d: d.age > 0),
}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
grays = ["#8E7F88", "#A9999F", "#C3B6BC", "#7A6A73", "#B5A6AD", "#9C8C94"]
for (lab, (f, k)), c in zip(TR.items(), grays):
    s = share(df, f, k, "year")
    ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color=c, lw=1.6)
    ax.text(2017.2, s.iloc[-1], lab, va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=MUTED)
ax.set_xlim(2005, 2021.5); ax.set_ylabel("% of exams")
ax.set_title("First try: six traits on one axis — hard to read")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Why this fails: the traits live on very different scales (HRT ~7–17%, density ~46%), so the small ones look flat, labels collide, and the eye has to match lines to names. Same data, worse reading. Better: small multiples — one small panel per trait, the same years on every x-axis, each y-axis starting at zero.

In [10]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 3, figsize=(12, 6.2), sharex=True)
for ax, (lab, (f, k)) in zip(axes.flat, TR.items()):
    s = share(df, f, k, "year")
    ax.plot(s.index, s.values, color=ROSE, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3.5)
    ax.set_title(f"{lab}\n{s.iloc[0]:.1f}% → {s.iloc[-1]:.1f}%", fontsize=11)
    ax.set_ylim(0, max(s.max() * 1.25, 5))
    ax.set_xticks([2005, 2009, 2013, 2017])
fig.supylabel("% of exams", color=MUTED)
fig.suptitle("Small multiples: every trait on its own scale, same years", x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

What I see:

  • HRT collapses in the first years — the after-effect of the 2002 Women's Health Initiative study that linked HRT to breast cancer. A risk factor that went the right way.
  • Obesity climbs steadily — a risk factor going the wrong way.
  • Non-White share rises — the patient mix is diversifying.
  • Prior breast cancer rises — survivors are a growing group (RQ3).
  • Density barely moves overall (but see section 6 — it hides big differences inside).

Next step: six panels are clear, but for a story I want one glance that answers "what changed most?". Third try: a dumbbell chart — one row per trait, first year vs last year, sorted by the size of the change.

In [11]:
rows = []
for lab, (f, k) in TR.items():
    s_ = share(df, f, k, "year")
    rows.append((lab, s_.iloc[0], s_.iloc[-1]))
rows.sort(key=lambda r: -(r[2] - r[1]))
lab, a, b = zip(*rows)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 3.9))
dumbbell(ax, lab, a, b, "2005", "2017")
ax.set_xlabel("% of exams (where known)"); ax.legend(loc="upper right")
ax.set_title(f"What shifted most 2005 → 2017: {rows[0][0]}, {rows[0][1]:.1f}% → {rows[0][2]:.1f}%")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Why this works better: the change itself (the grey bar and the number) is the data-ink; sorting puts the answer at the top. Dashboard decision: this is chart 1a of the app, and the years slider there lets the user choose the "first" and "last" year.

Three of these trends deserve a closer look: race (who is diversifying?), HRT (did it fall for everyone?) and obesity (is it rising for everyone?).

5e. Did hormone therapy fall for every age?¶

In [13]:
AGE_RAMP = ["#E58EA9", "#D0527A", "#A83A63", "#7A2B5B", "#4A1D3F"]
post = df[(df.meno == 2) & (df.hrt != 9)]
h = share(post, lambda d: d.hrt == 1, lambda d: d.hrt != 9, ["band", "year"]).unstack(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.2))
show = [b for b in BANDS if b != "<40"]
ys = spread([h[b].iloc[-1] for b in show], 2.2)
for b, y in zip(show, ys):
    c = AGE_RAMP[BANDS.index(b)]
    ax.plot(h.index, h[b], color=c, lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
    ax.text(2017.25, y, b, va="center", color=INK, fontsize=9.5)
ax.set_xlim(2004.6, 2018.4); ax.set_ylim(0, None); ax.set_ylabel("% on HRT (post-menopausal)")
ax.set_title("HRT fell in every age band from 40 up — the youngest post-menopausal women still use it most")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Thought: direct labels at the line ends replace a legend box (less eye travel). Colour goes light → dark with age because age is ordered. Under-40 is left out: very few post-menopausal women under 40.

5f. Is obesity rising for everyone?¶

In [14]:
ob_r = share(df[(df.race != 9) & (df.bmi != 9)], lambda d: d.bmi.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.bmi != 9,
             ["race", "year"]).unstack(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 4.3))
ys = spread([ob_r[c].iloc[-1] for c in [1, 2, 3, 5, 6]], 2.6)
for c, y in zip([1, 2, 3, 5, 6], ys):
    ax.plot(ob_r.index, ob_r[c], color=RACE_COL[c], lw=2.2, marker="o", ms=3)
    ax.text(2017.25, y, RACE[c], va="center", fontsize=9.5, color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(2004.6, 2019.2); ax.set_ylim(0, None); ax.set_ylabel("% with BMI ≥ 30 (BMI known)")
ax.set_title(f"Obesity rises in every group; Black women start highest ({ob_r[2].iloc[0]:.0f}%) "
             f"and end at {ob_r[2].iloc[-1]:.0f}%")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: obesity rises for every group, but from very different starting points. That means one prevention message does not fit all — an early hint of the business angle (targeted outreach).

6. RQ2 — Who has dense breasts?¶

Density is graded A (almost all fat) to D (extremely dense). Dense tissue looks white on a mammogram, like a tumour, so cancers can hide. Since 2024 U.S. clinics must tell women their density, so this matters for providers.

6a. Density by age¶

In [15]:
known = df[df.dens != 9]
t = known.groupby(["age", "dens"])["count"].sum().unstack()
t = 100 * t.div(t.sum(axis=1), axis=0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4.4))
bottom = np.zeros(len(t))
names = {1: "A · fatty", 2: "B · scattered", 3: "C · heterogeneously dense", 4: "D · extremely dense"}
for i, c in enumerate([1, 2, 3, 4]):
    ax.bar(range(len(t)), t[c], bottom=bottom, color=DENS_RAMP[i], width=0.8, label=names[c], edgecolor="white", lw=1)
    bottom += t[c].values
ax.set_xticks(range(len(t)), [AGE_LAB[a] for a in t.index])
ax.set_ylabel("% of exams (density known)")
dense = t[3] + t[4]
ax.set_title(f"Dense breasts (C+D) fall from {dense.iloc[0]:.0f}% of the youngest women to {dense.iloc[-1]:.0f}% at 85+")
ax.legend(ncol=4, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.1))
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Clear and strong: density fades with age. That confirms the first part of H2.

6b. Density by race — first try¶

In [16]:
kr = df[(df.dens != 9) & (df.race != 9)]
raw_r = share(kr, lambda d: d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9, "race")
young = share(df[df.race != 9], lambda d: d.age <= 5, lambda d: d.age > 0, "race")
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11, 3.8))
lab = [RACE[c] for c in raw_r.index]
axes[0].barh(lab, raw_r.values, color=[RACE_COL[c] for c in raw_r.index], height=0.6)
axes[0].set_title("Raw % with dense breasts"); axes[0].invert_yaxis()
axes[1].barh(lab, young.values, color=LIGHT, height=0.6)
axes[1].set_title("…but % of exams from women under 50 also differs"); axes[1].invert_yaxis()
for ax, v in zip(axes, (raw_r, young)):
    for i, x in enumerate(v.values):
        ax.text(x + 0.8, i, f"{x:.0f}%", va="center", fontsize=9.5)
    ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Problem: the groups have different age mixes. A group with more young women will look "denser" just because young breasts are denser (6a). So the left chart mixes two things: race and age. This is called confounding.

6c. Race × age — compare women of the same age¶

If I compared races directly, a group with more young women would look "denser" just because of age. A heatmap of race by age band removes that trap.

In [17]:
k = df[(df.dens != 9) & (df.race != 9)]
h = share(k, lambda d: d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9, ["race", "band"]).unstack()
h.index = [RACE[r] for r in h.index]
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.9))
im = ax.imshow(h.values, cmap=mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("rose", ["#FBEAF0", ROSE, PLUM]), aspect="auto")
for i in range(h.shape[0]):
    for j in range(h.shape[1]):
        v = h.values[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", color="white" if v > 52 else INK, fontsize=10.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(h.shape[1]), h.columns); ax.set_yticks(range(h.shape[0]), h.index)
ax.grid(False); ax.set_xlabel("Age band")
best = h.mean(axis=1).idxmax()
ax.set_title(f"% dense by race and age: {best} women are the densest in every age band")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="% dense", fraction=0.03)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: within every age band, Asian / Pacific Islander women have the highest share of dense breasts. The comparison also changes the picture for Hispanic women: in the raw chart they look the same as White women (46%), but they are younger on average (39% of exams under 50). At the same age they are less dense from 50 on. That is a real segment for supplemental-imaging conversations (ultrasound, 3D mammography) — and for language and outreach planning.

Second view of the same heatmap: the raw % is dominated by age (every row fades to the right). To make the race difference pop, I subtract the all-women value for that age band — a gap heatmap with a diverging scale.

In [18]:
allb = share(k, lambda d: d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9, "band")
gaph = h - allb.values
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.9))
lim = np.nanmax(np.abs(gaph.values))
im = ax.imshow(gaph.values, cmap=mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", [BLUE, "#F2F0F1", ROSE]),
               vmin=-lim, vmax=lim, aspect="auto")
for i in range(gaph.shape[0]):
    for j in range(gaph.shape[1]):
        v = gaph.values[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:+.0f}", ha="center", va="center", color="white" if abs(v) > lim * 0.6 else INK, fontsize=10.5)
ax.set_xticks(range(gaph.shape[1]), gaph.columns); ax.set_yticks(range(gaph.shape[0]), gaph.index)
ax.grid(False); ax.set_xlabel("Age band")
ax.set_title("Gap vs. all women of the same age (points): Asian / PI always above, Hispanic below from 50")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.03, label="points")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Thought: same data, different question. The raw view answers "how dense is this group?"; the gap view answers "how different is this group from its age peers?". Dashboard decision: the app has both, with a toggle.

6d. Density and BMI¶

Heavier women tend to be older in this data, so I compare BMI groups at the same age mix (direct age-standardisation: compute the rate inside each age group, then average with the same age weights).

In [19]:
def age_std(d, group, flag, known):
    # % with `flag` per group, re-weighted to the overall age mix of d
    d = d.assign(_n=d["count"] * flag(d), _d=d["count"] * known(d))
    t = d.groupby([group, "age"])[["_n", "_d"]].sum()
    rate = (t._n / t._d).unstack(0)
    wts = d.groupby("age")._d.sum(); wts = wts / wts.sum()
    return 100 * rate.mul(wts, axis=0).sum() / rate.notna().mul(wts, axis=0).sum()

BMI = {1: "< 25", 2: "25–29.9", 3: "30–34.9", 4: "35+"}
kb = df[(df.bmi != 9) & (df.dens != 9)]
raw_b = share(kb, lambda d: d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9, "bmi")
std_b = age_std(kb, "bmi", lambda d: d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9)
x = np.arange(4)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.9))
ax.bar(x - 0.2, raw_b.values, 0.4, color=LIGHT, label="Raw")
ax.bar(x + 0.2, std_b.values, 0.4, color=ROSE, label="Age-standardised")
for i, v in enumerate(std_b.values):
    ax.text(i + 0.2, v + 1, f"{v:.0f}%", ha="center", color=INK)
ax.set_xticks(x, [f"BMI {BMI[b]}" for b in raw_b.index]); ax.set_ylabel("% dense")
ax.set_title(f"Even at the same age, dense breasts drop from {std_b.iloc[0]:.0f}% (BMI < 25) to {std_b.iloc[-1]:.0f}% (BMI 35+)")
ax.legend(); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: the BMI–density link survives age adjustment, so H2 holds on all three parts (age, BMI, race). Lesson for me: age adjustment is needed throughout this dataset. The dashboard uses it in chapters 4–6.

7. RQ3 & RQ4 — Survivors and risk markers¶

Careful: this dataset has no new diagnoses and no deaths. It only says whether a woman has had breast cancer before. So I can study survivors who come back for screening, and which markers go with a past diagnosis. These are associations, not causes.

7a. Is the survivor rise just ageing?¶

In [20]:
kc = df[df.bch != 9]
obs = share(kc, lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9, "year")
adj = age_std(kc, "year", lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
ax.plot(obs.index, obs.values, color=ROSE, lw=2.4, marker="o", ms=4, label="As observed")
ax.plot(adj.index, adj.values, color=BLUE, lw=2.4, marker="o", ms=4, label="Age mix held fixed")
ax.text(obs.index[-1] + 0.15, obs.iloc[-1], f"{obs.iloc[-1]:.1f}%", va="center", color=INK)
ax.text(adj.index[-1] + 0.15, adj.iloc[-1], f"{adj.iloc[-1]:.1f}%", va="center", color=INK)
ax.set_xlim(2004.5, 2018.2); ax.set_ylim(0, obs.max() * 1.25)
ax.set_ylabel("% of exams from women with prior breast cancer")
part = 100 * (1 - (adj.iloc[-1] - adj.iloc[0]) / (obs.iloc[-1] - obs.iloc[0]))
ax.set_title(f"Survivors: {obs.iloc[0]:.1f}% → {obs.iloc[-1]:.1f}% of exams; ageing explains only ~{part:.0f}% of the rise")
ax.legend(loc="lower right"); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: H3 holds. Even if the age mix had not changed, survivors would still be a clearly rising share. Business meaning: a growing, loyal, high-need group — the case for a survivorship track in the dashboard.

Next question: where (which ages) are the survivors? A line per age would be 13 lines again, so I use a heatmap: age down the side, year across, colour = survivor share.

In [21]:
sh = share(kc, lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9, ["age", "year"]).unstack()
sh = sh.loc[4:]                     # 40+ (screening ages)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10.5, 4.6))
im = ax.imshow(sh.values, cmap=mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("rose", ["#FBEAF0", ROSE, PLUM]), aspect="auto")
for i in range(sh.shape[0]):
    for j in range(sh.shape[1]):
        v = sh.values[i, j]
        ax.text(j, i, f"{v:.0f}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color="white" if v > 17 else INK)
ax.set_xticks(range(sh.shape[1]), sh.columns); ax.set_yticks(range(sh.shape[0]), [AGE_LAB[a] for a in sh.index])
ax.grid(False)
ax.set_title("Survivor share (% of exams) by age and year: darkest at 75+, and every row darkens over time")
plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.025, label="%")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: the survivor share is highest in the oldest groups (expected — more years to have had a diagnosis), but the rows also get darker from left to right within the same age. That is the same message as 7a, seen a second way.

7b. All risk markers at once (age-adjusted)¶

Which markers travel with a past diagnosis? For every level of every marker I compute the share of exams from women with a prior breast cancer, age-standardised (survivors are older, so raw numbers would mostly show age). A lollipop chart keeps the ink low: a thin stick and a dot instead of a heavy bar.

In [22]:
FACT = [("Family history", "fh", {0: "No", 1: "Yes"}),
        ("Breast density", "dens", {1: "A fatty", 2: "B scattered", 3: "C hetero.", 4: "D extreme"}),
        ("BMI", "bmi", {1: "< 25", 2: "25–29.9", 3: "30–34.9", 4: "35+"}),
        ("Hormone therapy †", "hrt", {0: "Not current", 1: "Current"}),
        ("Menopause †", "meno", {1: "Pre / peri", 2: "Post", 3: "Surgical"}),
        ("Race / ethnicity", "race", RACE)]
overall = share(kc, lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9)
rows = []
for fname, col, levels in FACT:
    d = kc[kc[col] != 9]
    s_ = age_std(d, col, lambda x: x.bch == 1, lambda x: x.bch != 9)
    for code_, lab_ in levels.items():
        if code_ in s_.index:
            rows.append((fname, lab_, s_[code_]))
lol = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["factor", "level", "pct"])
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9.5, 7))
y = np.arange(len(lol))
ax.hlines(y, 0, lol.pct, color=LIGHT, lw=2)
ax.scatter(lol.pct, y, s=60, color=ROSE, edgecolor="white", lw=1.2, zorder=3)
for yi, v in zip(y, lol.pct):
    ax.text(v + 0.25, yi, f"{v:.1f}%", va="center", fontsize=9)
ax.set_yticks(y, [f"{f} · {l}" for f, l in zip(lol.factor, lol.level)], fontsize=9)
ax.invert_yaxis(); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
for i in np.where(lol.factor.ne(lol.factor.shift()))[0][1:]:
    ax.axhline(i - 0.5, color=GRID, lw=1)
ax.axvline(overall, color=PLUM, ls="--", lw=1.2)
ax.text(overall, -1.1, f"overall {overall:.1f}%", color=PLUM, ha="center", fontsize=9)
fy, fn_ = lol.set_index(["factor", "level"]).pct[("Family history", "Yes")], lol.set_index(["factor", "level"]).pct[("Family history", "No")]
ax.set_xlabel("% of exams from women with a prior breast cancer (age-standardised)")
ax.set_title(f"Family history: {fy:.1f}% vs {fn_:.1f}% — about {fy / fn_:.1f}× higher at the same age", pad=18)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Reading it: family history is the clearest marker. † marks things that can be a result of a diagnosis rather than a cause: many survivors stop HRT on medical advice, and some have surgical menopause as part of treatment. So those rows must not be read as risk factors. Density and BMI differences are small after age adjustment.

Dashboard decision: this is chart 5a of the app, with the † note. Family history deserves a zoom-in.

7c. Zoom in: family history at every age¶

In [23]:
kf = df[(df.bch != 9) & (df.fh != 9)]
fh = share(kf, lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9, ["fh", "age"]).unstack(0)
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 4))
ax.plot(range(len(fh)), fh[1], color=ROSE, lw=2.4, marker="o", label="Mother / sister / daughter had breast cancer")
ax.plot(range(len(fh)), fh[0], color=BLUE, lw=2.4, marker="o", label="No family history")
ax.set_xticks(range(len(fh)), [AGE_LAB[a] for a in fh.index])
ax.set_ylabel("% with prior breast cancer")
gap = fh[1] - fh[0]
ax.set_title(f"From age 40, family history goes with more prior cancer; the gap grows from "
             f"{gap.iloc[3]:.1f} pts (40–44) to {gap.iloc[-2]:.1f} pts (80–84)")
ax.axvspan(-0.5, 2.5, color=GRID, alpha=0.45, lw=0)
ax.text(1, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.55, "under 40:\nfew exams,\nnoisy", ha="center", color=MUTED, fontsize=9)
ax.legend(loc="upper left"); ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: H4 is only partly right. From age 40 on, the family-history line is above the other line in every age group and the gap widens with age. Under 40 it flips — but under-40 exams are only about 3% of the data, so those points are noisy and I do not read much into them. I had to rewrite my claim from "at every age" to "at every screening age (40+)". Family history is also the easiest question to ask at the front desk.

7d. A dead end I dropped: prior biopsy¶

In [24]:
kb2 = df[(df.bx != 9) & (df.bch != 9)]
bx = share(kb2, lambda d: d.bch == 1, lambda d: d.bch != 9, "bx")
print(f"Prior cancer among women WITH a past biopsy:    {bx[1]:.1f}%")
print(f"Prior cancer among women WITHOUT a past biopsy: {bx[0]:.2f}%")
print(f"Ratio (raw, not age-adjusted): {bx[1] / bx[0]:.0f}x")

Prior cancer among women WITH a past biopsy:    26.0%
Prior cancer among women WITHOUT a past biopsy: 1.86%
Ratio (raw, not age-adjusted): 14x

Thought: this is the biggest gap in the whole dataset — but it is trivial. Almost every woman who had breast cancer had a biopsy to diagnose it. The biopsy is part of the diagnosis, not a risk marker. Showing it would squash every other bar on the chart and teach nothing, so I left it out of the dashboard and explain why in a note.

7e. How do survivors differ from other women?¶

Turning 7b around: instead of "which marker has more survivors", ask "what does the survivor patient look like?". A dumbbell again (other women vs survivors), first raw, then age-adjusted, because survivors are older.

In [25]:
PROF = {k_: v_ for k_, v_ in TR.items() if k_ not in ("Prior breast cancer", "Aged 65+")}
PROF["Family history"] = (lambda d: d.fh == 1, lambda d: d.fh != 9)
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 3.9), sharey=True)
for ax, mode in zip(axes, ["raw", "adj"]):
    rows = []
    for lab, (f, k_) in PROF.items():
        if mode == "raw":
            r_ = share(kc, f, k_, "bch")
        else:
            r_ = age_std(kc, "bch", f, k_)
        rows.append((lab, r_[0], r_[1]))
    if mode == "raw":
        rows.sort(key=lambda r: -(r[2] - r[1]))
        order = [r[0] for r in rows]
    else:
        rows = sorted(rows, key=lambda r: order.index(r[0]))
    lab, a, b = zip(*rows)
    dumbbell(ax, lab, a, b, "No prior cancer", "Survivors")
    ax.set_title("Raw" if mode == "raw" else "Age-adjusted (same age mix)", fontsize=11.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("% of exams")
axes[1].legend(loc="center right")
fig.suptitle("Survivors: much less HRT (medical advice), more family history; most other gaps shrink after age adjustment",
             x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Thought: putting raw and adjusted side by side shows how much of each gap is just age. The HRT gap stays large (survivors are told to avoid hormone therapy) — that is a consequence, not a cause. Family history stays higher. Dashboard decision: chart 6c of the app, with a raw / age-adjusted toggle. Prior biopsy is left out (see 7d).

7f. Putting it together: business segments¶

A provider plans by segment. I cut the exams into age band × race segments and ask three things at once: how big is it (bubble size), how dense (x) and how many survivors (y).

In [26]:
seg = df[(df.race != 9)].assign(
    _n=lambda d: d["count"], _dn=lambda d: d["count"] * d.dens.isin([3, 4]), _dd=lambda d: d["count"] * (d.dens != 9),
    _sv=lambda d: d["count"] * (d.bch == 1), _sd=lambda d: d["count"] * (d.bch != 9))
g = seg.groupby(["band", "race"], observed=True)[["_n", "_dn", "_dd", "_sv", "_sd"]].sum()
g = g[g._n >= 5000]
g["dense"], g["surv"] = 100 * g._dn / g._dd, 100 * g._sv / g._sd
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5.8))
for (band, race), row in g.iterrows():
    size = 40 + row._n / 2000
    ax.scatter(row.dense, row.surv, s=size, color=AGE_RAMP[BANDS.index(band)], alpha=0.88, edgecolor="white", lw=1.2)
    ax.annotate(RACE[race][0], (row.dense, row.surv), xytext=(np.sqrt(size) / 2 + 2, 0), textcoords="offset points",
                va="center", fontsize=8.5, color=INK)
for b, c in zip(BANDS, AGE_RAMP):
    ax.scatter([], [], s=80, color=c, label=b)
ax.legend(title="Age band  (bubble size = exams; W White, B Black, A Asian/PI, H Hispanic, O Other)",
          loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, -0.14), ncol=5, fontsize=9)
ax.set_xlabel("% with dense breasts"); ax.set_ylabel("% with prior breast cancer")
ax.set_title("Segments: young = dense but few survivors; old = less dense, many survivors (letter = race)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
g.assign(exams=g._n.astype(int))[["exams", "dense", "surv"]].round(1).sort_values("exams", ascending=False).head(8)

Reading it: the bubbles fall into a diagonal from top-left (old: low density, many survivors) to bottom-right (young: dense, few survivors). Inside each age colour, the Asian / PI bubble (A) sits furthest right — the density finding from 6c again. The biggest bubbles (White women 50–69) are the core business; the smaller, fast-growing segments are where a targeted message can stand out.

Dashboard decision: this became the bubble chart and the persona builder in chapter 7 ("Business").

7g. Where does the volume sit? (mosaic)¶

The bubble chart is good for comparing segments, but it is hard to see how much of the business each one is. A mosaic (Marimekko) chart shows that directly: column width = share of exams in the age band, height inside the column = dense vs. not dense, colour = survivor share. Every area is proportional to exam volume.

In [27]:
mz = df[(df.dens != 9) & (df.bch != 9)].assign(dg=lambda d: np.where(d.dens >= 3, "Dense", "Not dense"),
                                               _sv=lambda d: d["count"] * (d.bch == 1))
m = mz.groupby(["band", "dg"], observed=True)[["count", "_sv"]].sum()
m["surv"] = 100 * m._sv / m["count"]
tot = m["count"].sum()
cmap = mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("rose", ["#FBEAF0", ROSE, PLUM])
norm = mpl.colors.Normalize(m.surv.min(), m.surv.max())
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 5))
x0 = 0
for band in BANDS:
    sub_ = m.loc[band]
    w = sub_["count"].sum() / tot
    y0 = 0
    for dg in ["Dense", "Not dense"]:
        h_ = sub_.loc[dg, "count"] / sub_["count"].sum()
        sv = sub_.loc[dg, "surv"]
        ax.add_patch(plt.Rectangle((x0, y0), w, h_, facecolor=cmap(norm(sv)), edgecolor="white", lw=2))
        if w > 0.06:
            ax.text(x0 + w / 2, y0 + h_ / 2, f"{dg}\n{100 * w * h_:.0f}% of exams\n{sv:.1f}% survivors",
                    ha="center", va="center", fontsize=8.5, color="white" if norm(sv) > 0.5 else INK)
        y0 += h_
    ax.text(x0 + w / 2, -0.05, f"{band}\n({100 * w:.0f}%)", ha="center", va="top", fontsize=9.5, color=MUTED)
    x0 += w
ax.set_xlim(0, 1); ax.set_ylim(0, 1); ax.axis("off")
plt.colorbar(mpl.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap=cmap), ax=ax, fraction=0.025, label="% survivors")
big = m["count"].idxmax()
ax.set_title(f"Mosaic of the business: biggest block = {big[1].lower()} breasts aged {big[0]} "
             f"({100 * m['count'].max() / tot:.0f}% of exams)", pad=12)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Reading it: 50–59 is the widest column (about 30% of exams), with 40–49 and 60–69 next — the core of the business. Within each column the dense share shrinks with age, while the colour (survivors) darkens with age. Under-40 is a thin sliver.

Dashboard decision: in the app this became an interactive treemap (same idea: area = volume), where the user picks the colour measure from a dropdown and clicks to zoom into an age band.

7h. One persona over time (preview of the persona builder)¶

The last idea: pick one patient profile and ask "is her segment growing?". Example: women aged 60–69 with dense breasts.

In [28]:
known_d = df[df.dens != 9]
per = share(known_d, lambda d: (d.band == "60–69") & d.dens.isin([3, 4]), lambda d: d.dens != 9, "year")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 3.6))
ax.plot(per.index, per.values, color=ROSE, lw=2.4, marker="o", ms=4)
ax.set_ylim(0, per.max() * 1.3); ax.set_ylabel("% of exams (density known)")
ax.set_title(f"Persona '60–69, dense breasts': {per.iloc[0]:.1f}% → {per.iloc[-1]:.1f}% of exams "
             f"({per.iloc[-1] - per.iloc[0]:+.1f} pts)")
ax.grid(axis="x", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Thought: a static notebook can only show one persona at a time. That is exactly why the persona builder belongs in the dashboard: five dropdowns (age, race, density, BMI, family history) let a marketer build any profile and see its size, how it differs from the average, and this trend line — without writing code.

8. RQ5 — Where she lives: a map and demographic exploration¶

BCSC does not say which state an exam came from. To ask whether place matters (food, exercise, smoking, income, insurance differ a lot between states), I brought in a second public dataset:

  • NCI / CDC State Cancer Profiles: female breast-cancer new cases and deaths, age-adjusted, per 100,000 women, 2015.
  • BRFSS 2016 (CDC lifestyle survey): obesity, smoking, no physical activity, daily fruit, daily vegetables.
  • American Community Survey 2012–16 (Census): uninsured under 65, below 150% of poverty line, median family income, bachelor's degree.
  • Census 2010 state boundaries for the maps.

prepare_state_data.py builds data/us_state_context.csv and data/us_states.geojson from these. One row = one state (50 + D.C. = 51 rows).

I add one measure of my own: deaths per 100 new cases = death rate ÷ new-case rate × 100. A high value means a diagnosis more often ends in death — a rough signal of late detection and weaker access to care.

8a. First look at the numbers¶

In [29]:

st["region"] = st.abbr.map(REGION)
print(st.shape, "| regions:", st.region.value_counts().to_dict())
st.describe().T[["mean", "min", "max"]].round(1)

Thought: new-case rates range from about 104 to 146 per 100k — a 40% spread between states. Death rates sit in a narrow 17–23 band, but D.C. (28.5) is far outside it. I note D.C. as a possible outlier and come back to it in 8f: it is a city, not a state, so it may behave differently.

8b. The first map — where is breast cancer found?¶

A table of 51 numbers hides geography. A choropleth (states shaded by value) shows neighbours and regions at once. I draw the states myself from the boundary file (Albers equal-area projection, Alaska and Hawaii as insets) using statemap.py, so the map works offline.

In [31]:
import statemap
SHAPES, LABELS = statemap.load_state_shapes()
SEQ = mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("ibu_seq", ["#F6DCE5", "#E58EA9", "#D0527A", "#A83A63", "#7A2B5B", PLUM])
BLUESEQ = mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("ibu_blue", ["#E3E8F5", "#86b6ef", "#3987e5", "#1c5cab", "#0d366b"])


XMAX = max(x.max() for r in SHAPES.values() for x, _ in r)
SMALL = {"CT", "RI", "MA", "NH", "VT", "NJ", "DE", "MD", "DC"}   # too small to hold a label inside


def us_map(ax, col, title, cmap=SEQ, fmt="{:.0f}", n_label=3, cbar=True):
    # Choropleth of one state column. Labels the n highest and n lowest states;
    # small Northeast states get a call-out in the Atlantic so labels never overlap.
    v = st.set_index("state")[col]
    abbr = st.set_index("state").abbr
    norm = mpl.colors.Normalize(v.min(), v.max())
    for name, rings in SHAPES.items():
        for x, y in rings:
            ax.fill(x, y, color=cmap(norm(v[name])), ec="white", lw=0.35)
    picks = list(dict.fromkeys(list(v.nlargest(n_label).index) + list(v.nsmallest(n_label).index)))
    small = sorted([n for n in picks if abbr[n] in SMALL], key=lambda n: -LABELS[n][1])
    for name in picks:
        if name in small:
            continue
        cx, cy = LABELS[name]
        ax.text(cx, cy, f"{abbr[name]}\n{fmt.format(v[name])}", ha="center", va="center", fontsize=7.2,
                color="white" if norm(v[name]) > 0.55 else INK, fontweight="bold")
    ty = None
    for name in small:
        cx, cy = LABELS[name]
        ty = cy if ty is None else min(cy, ty - 0.03)
        ax.annotate(f"{abbr[name]} {fmt.format(v[name])}", xy=(cx, cy), xytext=(XMAX + 0.03, ty), fontsize=7.4,
                    va="center", color=INK, fontweight="bold", arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=MUTED, lw=0.6))
    ax.set_xlim(right=XMAX + 0.13)
    ax.set_aspect("equal"); ax.axis("off")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=11.5)
    if cbar:
        plt.colorbar(mpl.cm.ScalarMappable(norm=norm, cmap=cmap), ax=ax, fraction=0.025, pad=0.01, shrink=0.75)


fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 6.2))
us_map(ax, "inc", "New breast-cancer cases per 100,000 women (2015): highest in the Northeast, lowest in the Mountain West")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

What I see: the darkest states cluster in the Northeast (New Hampshire, Connecticut, Massachusetts, Rhode Island). The lightest are in the Mountain West (Wyoming, Nevada, New Mexico, Arizona).

My first reaction was wrong: I almost wrote "the Northeast is the most dangerous place for breast cancer". But a new-case rate counts cancers that were found. States that screen more find more — including small, early cancers. So I need a second outcome: deaths.

8c. Found vs. lost — two more maps¶

In [32]:
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(13, 4.6))
us_map(axes[0], "mort", "Deaths per 100,000 women", fmt="{:.1f}")
us_map(axes[1], "mi", "Deaths per 100 new cases (my measure)", fmt="{:.1f}")
fig.suptitle("The death maps look different from the new-case map: the South and D.C. turn dark",
             x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Finding: the pattern flips. The Northeast, which had the most new cases, has the fewest deaths per 100 cases (Connecticut, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, New Hampshire). The South and D.C. have the most. Same disease, very different endings — this is the core of RQ5.

Design note: I used one hue (rose), light → dark for every map because each shows a magnitude ("more" = darker). A rainbow scale would add colour without adding meaning.

8d. Lifestyle and money, mapped¶

Now the "why" candidates. First lifestyle — the food / exercise / smoking side the question started from.

Thought: I switched the economic maps to blue so the eye knows these are the explanations, not the cancer outcomes (rose). Small multiples again: same projection, same size, so I can compare by glancing across.

What I see: many of the "bad" maps look alike — the South is dark for obesity, smoking, inactivity, poverty and uninsured. That is a warning: these factors travel together, so later I cannot easily say which one matters.

8e. Regions — a ranked view¶

Maps make big states (Texas, Montana) look important just because they are big. A ranked dot plot gives every state the same space. I colour the dots by Census region.

8f. Which factors line up with which outcome? (correlation heatmap)¶

In [36]:
NAMES = {"inc": "New cases", "mort": "Deaths", "mi": "Deaths / 100 cases", "obese": "Obesity", "smoke": "Smoking",
         "inactive": "Inactivity", "fruit": "Daily fruit", "veg": "Daily veg", "unins": "Uninsured", "pov": "Poverty",
         "income": "Income", "bach": "Degree"}
outc, ctx = ["inc", "mort", "mi"], ["obese", "smoke", "inactive", "fruit", "veg", "unins", "pov", "income", "bach"]
div = mpl.colors.LinearSegmentedColormap.from_list("div", [BLUE, "#F2F0F1", ROSE])


def corr_heat(d, title):
    corr = d[outc + ctx].corr().loc[outc, ctx]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(11, 3.2))
    im = ax.imshow(corr.values, cmap=div, vmin=-1, vmax=1, aspect="auto")
    for i in range(corr.shape[0]):
        for j in range(corr.shape[1]):
            v = corr.values[i, j]
            ax.text(j, i, f"{v:+.2f}", ha="center", va="center", color="white" if abs(v) > 0.5 else INK, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_xticks(range(len(ctx)), [NAMES[c] for c in ctx]); ax.set_yticks(range(3), [NAMES[c] for c in outc])
    ax.grid(False); ax.set_title(title)
    plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, fraction=0.025, label="r")
    plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
    return corr

c_all = corr_heat(st, "All 51: money and insurance line up with breast cancer more than lifestyle does")

Thought: a diverging scale (blue = negative, grey = 0, rose = positive) because the sign matters here.

At first this looks like H5a fails: obesity, smoking and inactivity barely relate to anything (|r| < 0.3). But I flagged D.C. as an outlier in 8a — a city with low obesity and the highest death rate. One extreme point can hide a pattern in 51 points. Robustness check: run it again without D.C.

In [37]:

pd.DataFrame({"with DC": c_all.stack(), "without DC": c_no.stack()}).assign(
    change=lambda t: t["without DC"] - t["with DC"]).round(2).sort_values("change", key=abs, ascending=False).head(6)

This changed my conclusion. Without D.C., obesity vs. death rate jumps from about +0.16 to about +0.45, and smoking and inactivity also strengthen. So lifestyle does line up with dying from breast cancer across the 50 states — D.C. was hiding it. Lifestyle still does not line up with new cases. The money side gets even stronger too: income and degree vs. deaths per 100 cases move to about −0.65 and −0.62.

Lesson: always check whether one point is driving (or hiding) a correlation.

8g. The two clearest relationships¶

In [38]:

                                       ("pov", "mi", "% below 150% of poverty line", "Deaths per 100 new cases")]):
    x, y = st[xk], st[yk]
    m, b = np.polyfit(x, y, 1)
    xx = np.array([x.min(), x.max()])
    ax.plot(xx, m * xx + b, color=LIGHT, lw=2, ls="--")

    for i in list({y.idxmax(), y.idxmin(), x.idxmax(), x.idxmin()}):
        ax.annotate(st.abbr[i], (x[i], y[i]), xytext=(4, 4), textcoords="offset points", color=MUTED, fontsize=9)
    ax.set_xlabel(xl); ax.set_ylabel(yl)
    ax.set_title(f"r = {np.corrcoef(x, y)[0, 1]:+.2f}", fontsize=11.5)
axes[0].xaxis.set_major_formatter(mpl.ticker.FuncFormatter(lambda v, _: f"{v/1000:.0f}k"))
for r_, c in REG_COL.items():
    axes[1].scatter([], [], color=c, s=34, label=r_)
axes[1].legend(loc="upper left", fontsize=9)
fig.suptitle("Richer states FIND more breast cancer; poorer states LOSE more women per case",
             x=0.01, ha="left", fontweight="bold", color=INK)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Reading it carefully:

  • More new cases in richer states most likely means more screening finds more cancer — not that money causes cancer.
  • More deaths per case where poverty is high fits later diagnosis and weaker access to care.
  • These are two separate charts on purpose: one y-axis each, never a dual axis.

8h. Can I separate the factors? A small model¶

Poverty, uninsured, obesity and smoking all move together (8d). To see which one still matters when the others are held fixed, I fit a small linear regression of deaths per 100 cases on all four, with every variable standardised (so the bars are comparable: "change in deaths per case, in standard deviations, for +1 SD of the factor").

In [39]:
def std_reg(d, xs, y):
    X = (d[xs] - d[xs].mean()) / d[xs].std()
    Y = (d[y] - d[y].mean()) / d[y].std()
    A = np.c_[np.ones(len(d)), X.values]
    beta = np.linalg.lstsq(A, Y.values, rcond=None)[0]
    r2 = 1 - ((Y - A @ beta) ** 2).sum() / ((Y - Y.mean()) ** 2).sum()
    return pd.Series(beta[1:], index=xs), r2

xs = ["pov", "unins", "obese", "smoke"]
b_all, r2_all = std_reg(st, xs, "mi")
b_no, r2_no = std_reg(st[st.abbr != "DC"], xs, "mi")
print("Correlation between the four factors:")
print(st[xs].corr().round(2).rename(index=NAMES, columns=NAMES), "\n")
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8.5, 3.6))
yy = np.arange(len(xs))
ax.barh(yy - 0.2, b_all.values, 0.38, color=LIGHT, label=f"All 51 (R² = {r2_all:.2f})")
ax.barh(yy + 0.2, b_no.values, 0.38, color=ROSE, label=f"Without D.C. (R² = {r2_no:.2f})")
ax.axvline(0, color=MUTED, lw=1)
ax.set_yticks(yy, [NAMES[x] for x in xs]); ax.invert_yaxis()
ax.set_xlabel("Standardised coefficient on deaths per 100 cases")
ax.set_title("Holding the others fixed, poverty stays the strongest factor")
ax.legend(loc="lower right"); ax.grid(axis="y", visible=False)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

Correlation between the four factors:
           Poverty  Uninsured  Obesity  Smoking
Poverty       1.00       0.46     0.51     0.49
Uninsured     0.46       1.00     0.32     0.17
Obesity       0.51       0.32     1.00     0.76
Smoking       0.49       0.17     0.76     1.00

Finding: poverty keeps the largest positive coefficient in both versions; uninsured comes second once D.C. is removed. Obesity's coefficient is small or even negative, although on its own obesity correlates positively with deaths per case. The reason: obesity and smoking are strongly correlated with each other and with poverty (r ≈ 0.5–0.76), so the model cannot split them apart (multicollinearity).

Honest limits: 51 data points, a single year, state averages (not individual women), and the model explains roughly 40–50% of the variation. This is a pointer, not proof. I did not put the model in the dashboard — it is too fragile — but it gave me confidence to say "poverty and access" in the story.

8i. What section 8 means for the business¶

  • Where income and insurance are high (Northeast): women already get screened and cancers are found early. The message is retention: keep your yearly appointment.
  • Where poverty is high and deaths per case are high (much of the South, D.C.): the barrier is access and cost — mobile mammography, sliding-scale prices, partnerships with churches and community groups, and transport.
  • One national campaign would miss both.

Dashboard decision: chapter 2 ("Geography") = an interactive map with a measure dropdown, a click-to-select state profile, and a scatter where the user picks both axes, so anyone can repeat 8b–8g themselves.

10. From this notebook to the dashboard¶

Exploration here What it became in the Dash app
Unknown-values chart (4) Rule: each measure uses only exams where it is known; two columns dropped. Explained in "More information about this data".
Exams per year (5a) Rule: show shares, not totals.
First try "spaghetti" chart → small multiples → dumbbell (5c) Dumbbell "what shifted most" (chapter 1).
HRT by age, obesity by race (5e, 5f) The two other charts of chapter 1, with direct labels.
Age mix, race mix (5b, 5d) "Screening is a midlife service" + 100% stacked race chart (chapter 3).
Density: naive race chart → race × age heatmap (% and gap), BMI (6) Chapter 4: density by age, heatmap with a % / gap toggle, BMI chart.
Survivor trend and heatmap (7a) Chapter 6: observed vs. age-fixed line, heatmap with a % / count toggle.
Risk-marker lollipop, family history by age (7b–7c) Chapter 5: both charts; biopsy dropped with a note (7d).
Survivor profile, raw vs. adjusted (7e) Chapter 6: dumbbell with a raw / age-adjusted toggle.
Segment bubbles, mosaic, one persona (7f–7h) Chapter 7: bubble chart, treemap, persona builder.
Maps, regions, correlations, D.C. check, scatter (8a–8g) Chapter 2: interactive map with a measure dropdown, click-to-select state profile, scatter with user-picked axes.
Small regression (8h) Not in the app (too fragile); used only to support the wording "poverty and access".

Limits to remember: exams, not women (one woman can appear in several years); associations, not causes; no new diagnoses or deaths in BCSC; facility participation changes over time; state data is from a different source and year (2015–16) and describes states, not women.

Next ideas: add stage at diagnosis (not in this dataset), link to county-level screening rates, and test whether the density segment grows after the 2024 FDA density-notification rule.
